description: Hello Everyone! We are a motivated team joining the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 from Türkiye, aiming for a Beginner/Intermediate project focused on the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Our current crew has a strong passion for space exploration, gamification, educational design, and clear storytelling. We value smooth communication, efficient time management, and a stress-free environment to ensure we deliver a fun and a completed work.
summary:
ASTROMOON is an interactive educational game that places players in charge of managing a lunar outpost during a 16-day mission. In the role of mission commander, players must make critical decisions and manage limited resources such as water, oxygen, energy, and food to ensure the safety of the outpost. Through different scenarios, they encounter challenges related to life-support systems, energy management, and plant cultivation for food production, and work to find solutions. Since each decision can affect multiple systems, the game demonstrates how closely the sustainability of a lunar outpost depends on balanced resource management.

ASTROMOON directly contributes to the goals of the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by transforming the complex responsibilities of astronauts during a lunar mission into an interactive learning experience. Rather than simply learning about space exploration, players actively make decisions and experience their possible consequences. The project aims to make the scientific and practical challenges of future lunar missions more accessible to young learners while developing their critical thinking, problem-solving, and resource-management skills.
details:
1. What Does Your Project Do, and How Does It Work?

Our project is a browser-based resource-management simulation that puts players in the role of the commander of a lunar base. Players must survive a 16-day mission by managing five critical resources: water, oxygen, energy, food, and health. The game has two layers: a pre-mission briefing (terrain selection, fertilizer selection, and seed selection) and in-game scenarios (events such as a new plant species, dust accumulating on solar panels, a meteorite impact, and plant-health problems). With every choice, players must make trade-offs between resources. For example, planting a high-yield crop quickly increases the food supply, but consumes more energy and water. The game allows players to see the consequences of their decisions in real time.

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

The benefits of our project include:

• Education: It teaches players about the challenges of surviving in space, resource management, and decision-making in an engaging way.

• Awareness: Drawing on real data from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) and NASA, it demonstrates the practical relevance of space agriculture, including hydroponics, fertilizer selection, and radiation protection.

• Inspiration for Young People: It aims to encourage young people, particularly those aged 8–14, to explore STEM fields. Through the “Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” concept, it seeks to inspire them to become the scientists and engineers of the future.

• Replayability and Exploration: By choosing different terrain, fertilizers, and crops, and encountering different in-game scenarios, players can try a variety of strategies. This encourages replayability and exploration, while prompting players to wonder, “What would have happened if I had chosen the other option?” The feedback provided at the end of the game also gives players an opportunity to develop a better strategy for their next playthrough. We believe this is a particularly valuable feature in educational games.

• Direct Connection to Earth: Using the CSA and other resources consulted for the project, we provide an information card at the end of the game, helping players connect the gameplay with real-world data. Players learn through experience how choices such as fertilizer selection affect crop yield and resource consumption. This brings real information from the CSA resources “Interplanetary Farming” and “Deep Space Food Challenge” into the game.

• Behavioral Benefits: As players try to survive for 16 days with limited resources, they develop skills in stress management, prioritization, and rapid decision-making. This is a valuable cognitive exercise, especially for young people.

• An Accessible Educational Tool: Because our game is desktop-based and developed in Python:

• It does not require an internet connection and can run on a computer in many settings.

• Teachers can use it as a classroom activity—for example, by asking students to play the game and discuss which strategy works best.

• It is free, making it accessible to everyone.

3. What Is the Intended Impact?

Our intended impact is to turn an abstract concept such as “survival in space” into a concrete game that young people can understand. In addition, the game’s core idea of surviving with limited resources is intended to help players recognize the connection between gameplay and the data in the sources we use.

4. What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use to Develop Your Project? We used the following tools and technologies to develop our project:

• Programming Language: Python, used to create a game that can be accessed by users. • Development Environment: Visual Studio Code.

• Design: We first examined real images of the Moon from NASA. We then used Claude to interpret these images and integrated them into the code with the Pygame library.

• Hardware: A standard laptop; no specialized hardware was required.

5. How Is Your Project Creative?

The creativity of our project comes from combining a resource-management mechanic with real space science. Our work presents players with multi-layered decisions, while the scenarios they encounter refer to real-world research. The game’s Decision Matrix mechanic allows players to clearly see the consequences of each choice. This makes the experience both educational and entertaining.

6. What Factors, Such as Energy, Accessibility, or Cost, Did Your Team Consider? Our team considered the following factors:

• Educational Value: We made the game both entertaining and educational, helping players understand the challenges of lunar life, resource management, and sustainability in space.

• Replayability: We introduced different starting options and changing crisis scenarios to encourage players to explore alternative strategies and learn from each playthrough.

• Technical Feasibility: We considered our development timeline, technical capabilities, and available resources to ensure the game would run smoothly and reliably.

• Accessibility: Our game is desktop-based and runs in Python, so it can be used on a computer accessible to a wide range of users. It also works offline.

• Cost: Our game was developed entirely using free tools, including Python. It does not require specialized hardware or paid licenses.

• Realism: We maintained a scientific foundation by incorporating real challenges of lunar life and space missions into the game scenarios.

ASTROMOON: Game Overview

ASTROMOON is a strategy- and resource-management-based survival simulation in which the player manages a research base established on the lunar surface. The player takes responsibility for the base on the Moon and must carefully manage limited resources to keep the astronaut alive. The main objective is to keep the base’s life-support systems operational throughout the mission, respond to emerging crises by making sound decisions, and complete the mission while protecting the astronaut’s health.

1. Starting the Game and Preparation

At the beginning of the game, the player makes three key preparation choices. These choices affect resource consumption and production capacity in the days that follow.

• Plant Selection: The player chooses one of three crops to grow in the greenhouse: potatoes, lettuce, or carrots. Each crop has different nutritional value, growth rate, and resource requirements.

• Fertilizer Selection: The player chooses between organic and mineral fertilizer. Each type has different water and energy requirements.

• Base Location Selection: A sunny area offers an advantage in energy production. The edge of a crater offers the advantage of being close to water ice, but receives less sunlight and is therefore less favorable for energy production. Flat terrain provides a more balanced starting point.

Once these three choices have been made, the main survival phase begins.

2. Resource Management

Resource management is the game’s most important mechanic. The player must continuously monitor four essential resources and the astronaut’s health; if health reaches zero, the mission fails.. The resources are water, oxygen, energy and food.

Water is Used for the astronaut’s needs and for watering plants. Oxygen is Required for the astronaut to breathe and produced by plants. Indicates the astronaut’s overall condition. Energy is Generated by solar panels and used by systems such as greenhouse lighting. Food is Obtained from plants grown in the greenhouse and provides nutrition for the astronaut. Resource values range from 0 to 120, and the initial level of each primary resource is 100. Each game turn represents one day. At the end of each day, resources are automatically consumed or replenished. Resources are interdependent. For example, more water and energy can be used to produce more food in the greenhouse. However, this may reduce the resources available to other life-support systems.

3. Daily Gameplay Loop

The game progresses day by day. Each day, the player reviews the current resource levels, evaluates any events that arise, and proceeds to the next day.

• The player checks the current levels of water, oxygen, energy, food, and health. • The player checks whether a crisis has occurred that day.

• If a crisis occurs, the player chooses one of the two options presented. • The effects of the decision on resources are applied.

• Daily resource consumption and production take place.

• A new day begins, and the resource levels are checked again. The player does not need to perform a direct action every day. Daily changes in resources happen automatically. Therefore, the game is built around continuous resource monitoring, good timing, and long-term planning.

4. Crises and the Decision-Making System

One of the game’s key features is the player’s ability to respond to unexpected events. There are five different crisis scenarios throughout the game. Their order is determined randomly. The first crisis occurs on Day 3, and subsequent crises take place at intervals of 2–3 days. For each crisis, the player is offered two possible solutions. The player determines the outcome by choosing one of them. However, no decision is entirely beneficial: protecting one resource may require sacrificing another.

A. Meteorite Impact A meteorite strikes the base, causing an oxygen leak in the life-support section. The player can send the astronaut outside to repair the damage or isolate the damaged section. The first option reduces the astronaut’s health and energy, while the second reduces oxygen production and the base’s capacity.

B. Disease in the Greenhouse A disease that spreads rapidly among the plants appears. The player can use energy to apply treatment and pause production for one turn. Alternatively, the player can isolate the affected section; however, food losses continue in this case.

C. Increased Greenhouse Water Requirements As the plants enter a period of rapid growth, their water requirements increase. The player can allocate water to the greenhouse to protect food production or prioritize the astronaut’s drinking water. Both decisions have long-term consequences.

D. Lunar Dust and Solar Panels A dust storm on the lunar surface reduces the efficiency of the solar panels. The player can sacrifice some of the astronaut’s health to have the panels cleaned or use backup energy to postpone dealing with the problem.

E. New Plant Species or Conventional Farming The player is informed that a new plant species will be sent from Earth. The player can choose the new plant, which provides high food production but consumes a large amount of water and energy, or continue with conventional farming, which uses fewer resources. This decision directly affects the resource balance in subsequent turns.

5. When Resources Fall to Critical Levels Solving crises alone is not enough; the player must also continuously monitor daily resource levels. In the game, 20 points is defined as the critical threshold.

• If water, oxygen, or food falls below 20, the astronaut’s health decreases by 5 points each day.

• If energy falls below 20, plant production decreases by 50%.

• If the astronaut’s health reaches zero, the mission ends. This system requires the player to think about long-term sustainability rather than short-term gains. For example, using too much water to increase food production may put the astronaut’s drinking-water supply at risk in the following days.

6. Game Ending and Scoring System

The game lasts a total of 16 days. Throughout this period, the player tries to protect the astronaut’s health while managing resources.

Success Condition

The player must complete the 16-day period without the astronaut’s health falling to zero.

Failure Condition

The mission ends if the astronaut’s health reaches zero. When the mission is completed, the player receives a four-page mission report containing:

• Number of days survived

• Lowest resource levels reached during the mission

• Final resource values • Graphs showing daily changes in resources

• The player’s decisions during crises • Suggestions for improvement in the next playthrough. The game’s scoring system is based on three main criteria: Number of days survived(40% weight), Final health value(40% weight), Average resource level(30% weight). In addition, every day spent at a critical resource level negatively affects the score. If the mission fails, the maximum possible score is capped at 35.
dataRefs: 1. NASA Open APIs - Provides access to various NASA data services, including information about near-Earth objects and asteroids. Used as a starting point for researching celestial objects and their orbits.

3. NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) - Contains biological research data from spaceflight experiments, including studies involving plants, water stress, and other living organisms. Relevant examples include the VEG-01A and OSD-766 studies.

4. NASA  Growing Plants in Space - Explains plant cultivation in space, including NASA’s Veggie system aboard the International Space Station, lighting, water, nutrients, and controlled growing conditions.
5. NASA Plant Biology Program - Provides scientific background on plant growth, development, and responses to environmental conditions.
6. NASA Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) - Explains life support systems, including cabin air, oxygen production, carbon dioxide removal, and water management.
projectRefs: Canadian Space Agency Food Production Toolkit - Provides educational information about food production in space and on the Moon, astronaut nutrition, plant cultivation, and water recycling.
